summary.value: The paper proposes applying "transfer entropy" (TE) to study the flow of information across layers over time in language and vision-language models.  They derive an approximation to the TE (as computing it directly is infeasible) and use it to make some observations/suggest the following applications: (1) layers that are less "informative", as suggested by TE, can be removed, leading to a smaller model with similar performance; (2) vision and text models display differing characteristic trends in the information flow

strengths.value:
1. The proposed TE + approximation method (conditioned on the mathematical correctness, see Weaknesses) is interesting and promises to be useful in understanding the inner workings of such models in the future.
2. The experiments use TE to provide interesting observations, such as vision models displaying hierarchical organization of information in layers.
3. As an application of TE, the paper also proposes a method for model pruning, which is a relevant practically important problem.

weaknesses.value:
1. The presentation of mathematical details in Sections 3 and 4 is rather poor (see Questions).

2. This might be an artifact of the poor presentation, but I cannot verify that the statements claimed in Section 4 are correct (again, see Questions).  Thus, though the experiments suggest that the method "works", I cannot be sure that it is working for the intended reasons.  As such, I cannot recommend acceptance, but I will be happy to improve my score if my questions are addressed satisfactorily.

questions.value:
1. How does TE compare with Granger causality (GC)?  Though GC is mentioned in related works, it is not clear what exactly differentiates GC and TE (their features are simply listed without direct comparison, either quantitative or qualitative).  Comments on what TE gives that GC does not?

2. What exactly is the perturbation in Section 4.2? Are you assuming that (X^{t+1}_{l}, X^{t+1}_{l+1}) approx (X^{t}_{l}, X^{t}_{l+1}) + delta x?  (i.e., in your model, is this "perturbation" affecting the value of X_{l} and X_{l+1} at the next instant?  If yes, then what is the need for the Jacobian matrices in (13) and (14)?  If not, i.e., if you mean delta x to be the perturbation at the same instant, then shouldn't y = X^{t}_{l+1} also change (i.e. not be deterministic, as is claimed)? 

4. Other examples of poor presentation/notation (most of this is minor but adds to the general difficulty in reading the paper): 
      1. Section 4.1:  There is no need to introduce u,y,v to denote different X's at t/t+1 and l/l+1, eqns (3), (4), (5) are also completely unnecessary --- TE_l(t) as given in (6) would have been completely fine, along with a possible comment that it is TE as in (2) evaluated between two processes: the activations at layer l shifted backwards in time by 1, and the activations at layer l+1;  Same section, h_l and h_{l+1} are introduced without description)
     2. Section 4.3:  \mathcal{T}, S^{prev} and S^{null} are new, no description.

comment.value: Thank you for your response.  No, I did mean y_0 + delta x_2, without the Jacobian (the Jacobian is for the transformation from time t to t+1, but y is the value at the same time t).  In any case, I disagree with the claim that you can simply replace y by y_0 in (36), consider the following scenario: Let a be a real valued constant, and let X, Y be random variables such that Y = a + X.  Let Z1, Z2 be independent of X, and let Wi = f(X,Zi) for some function f.  If I want to evaluate I(W1; W2 | X), your line of reasoning would say "given X, we have that Y is determined, as Y = a + X, and so we subtract Y from the arguments to get I(W1; W2 | a);  as a is a constant, this last expression is equal to I(W1; W2)", which is false (take the trivial example f(x,z) = x to see immediately why this is false --- I(W1; W2 | X) = 0, but I(W1; W2) = H(X)).  By subtracting delta x_2 from y, you are removing exactly the part of y that makes it random (as y_0 is a constant), then using this to later conclude that y is deterministic (or "held fixed", as you say).  Is there a mistake in my understanding?
Thank you for the revisions and clarifications. The concerns I raised about presentation have been addressed, I believe my original score remains appropriate.

Thank you for the discussion. We believe the shorthand $h(x)=f(x,g(x))$ with $x=X_{l+1}^{t}$ does not fully capture the structure of transfer entropy in our setting. In $TE_l(t)=I(X_{l+1}^{t+1};X_l^{t+1}\mid X_{l+1}^{t})$, there are three distinct random variables: the conditioning state $y:=X_{l+1}^{t}$, the source $v:=X_l^{t+1}$, and the target $u:=X_{l+1}^{t+1}$. Importantly, $(u,v)$ is not a single-variable function of $y$ alone: the source $v=X_l^{t+1}$ is produced by upstream computation (layer $l$) and is not generated by the $t\to t{+}1$ transition of layer $l{+}1$. Rather, the appropriate transition is of the form $u=g(y,v)$ (or $u=g(y,v,\xi)$ in a stochastic view), i.e., the next state at layer $l{+}1$ depends on both the prior state $y$ and the updated input $v$. Under this identification, one may write $f(y,(u,v)):=I(u;v\mid y)$ and view the composite as $h(y,v)=f\big(y,(g(y,v),v)\big)=I(g(y,v);v\mid y)$, which makes explicit that TE is a conditional MI with conditioner $y$ and source $v$ rather than a single-input map $x\mapsto g(x)$. Please let us know your thoughts. We appreciate your time and effort in this discussion.

title.value: Additional Experiments with Larger LLMs and Expanded Analysis

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive feedback and address each point below. The revised version of the paper incorporates substantial clarifications and new experiments.

W1: We appreciate the suggestion. In the revision, we added a new Section 5.2.2 in the main paper that summarizes and discusses our findings from Appendix H.2 and H.3 on role-aware token and head classification. The results are now integrated directly into the main narrative to make their relevance to our central claims clearer.

W2: We agree that additional evaluation is beneficial. Beyond GLUE, we included experiments on four Chain-of-Thought (CoT) datasets: e-SNLI, CQA, ANLI, and SVAMP for RoBERTa (Appendix G.5). Across these tasks, RoBERTa exhibits consistent information-flow patterns, indicating that our findings are not benchmark-specific.  We also expanded our analysis to a different architecture family, T5 (encoder-decoder), evaluated on twelve datasets (8 GLUE tasks + 4 CoT datasets). As shown in Appendix G.4 and G.5, T5 demonstrates qualitatively similar information-flow behavior for different datasets. We have added LLaVA-7B with datasets MSCOCO and Flick8k in Appendix H.1, which also demonstrate similar information-flow in different datasets.

W3: We appreciate the concern regarding smaller models. In response, we have added experiments on larger LLMs, including LLaMA-3B and Qwen-7B. The results are detailed in Appendix G.6.

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful feedback. Our detailed responses are provided below.

W1: Thank you for pointing this out. In the revision, we have expanded the main text by adding Section 5.1.3 and Section 5.2.2, which summarize the key empirical findings previously located only in the appendix. 

W2: We have thoroughly revised the manuscript to include explicit references to all corresponding appendix sections. Each major analysis is now clearly pointed to from the main text.

W3: Thank you. We have clarified the rationale in the first paragraph of Section 5.1. 

W4: We agree that TE estimation in high-dimensional networks warrants a clearer discussion. We have added Appendix J (Limitations) that addresses potential biases in the TE approximations, including local linearity assumptions, finite-batch noise, and the use of low-rank covariance surrogates. We also emphasize that our goal is to capture qualitative, layerwise trends rather than exact TE magnitudes.

W5: Thank you for pointing this out. We have added explicit cross-references to the expanded main text and appendix sections to ensure that readers can trace each part of the evidence supporting our claims.

Q1: We appreciate this question. These analyses are now summarized directly in the main paper in Section 5.2.2. The appendix H.2 and H.3 contain the token-level and head-level analyses.

Q2: The computational and statistical trade-offs between the Jacobian-based linear–Gaussian TE and the cosine-similarity approximation are compared in Appendix D. In brief:  
1) The Jacobian approximation is more principled but requires backpropagation and scales with hidden dimensionality.  
2) The cosine approximation is extremely lightweight, requiring only forward activations and operating in linear time, making it well-suited for large-scale models and online use. 

Q3: We have extended our experiments to larger decoder-only LLMs.  Appendix G.6 now includes results on Llama-3B and Qwen-7B. Appendix H.1 includes multimodal experiments on LLaVA-7B.  

Q4: Yes. As discussed at the end of Appendix D, the cosine-similarity TE estimator incurs only linear-time cost and negligible memory overhead. This makes online TE computation practical and compatible with standard training loops, including those used in LLM fine tuning.

title.value: Conditioning in TE and Local Perturbations

comment.value:
Thank you for the careful abstraction. In your shorthand $f(x_0, g(x_0+\delta x))$, the same symbol $x_0$ is used for both the conditioning variable $y$ and the source variable $v$. In our setting these are distinct quantities (with $y:=X_{l+1}^{t}$ and $v:=X_l^{t+1}$), so writing both as $x_0$ is not an accurate representation of our perturbation.

Similarly, your expression $h(x_0+\delta x)=f(x_0+\delta x, g(x_0+\delta x))$ again treats the same perturbed quantity as both the conditioner $y$ and the source $v$. In our formulation, the conditioner $y:=X_{l+1}^{t}$ is held fixed (to define the conditional slice in TE), while the perturbation is applied only to the source $v:=X_l^{t+1}$; thus a shared-$x$ update does not reflect the TE we compute. 

For additional clarity, note that $y=X_{l+1}^{t}$ plays different roles across adjacent indices: when estimating $TE_l(t-1)=I(X_{l+1}^{t};X_l^{t}\mid X_{l+1}^{t-1})$, $X_{l+1}^{t}$ is the future/target variable and thus varies across perturbation samples; when estimating $TE_l(t)$, $X_{l+1}^{t}$ is the **conditioning** variable (already **obtained in the last iteration**) and is therefore held fixed within that conditional MI estimate.

We appreciate your time and thoughtful feedback, and please let us know what you think.

summary.value: This paper introduces Transfer Entropy (TE) as a principled information-theoretic measure to quantify directional information flow and causal influence between layers, tokens, and attention heads in Transformer architectures. By developing tractable estimators (e.g., Jacobian approximations) for high-dimensional hidden states, the authors analyze information propagation patterns in LLMs and VLMs, proposing a novel pruning strategy based on low TE signals to enhance efficiency while preserving performance.

strengths.value:
## Strengths

1. **S1: Introduction of a Principled Causal Measure (Transfer Entropy).**
    The paper addresses a fundamental limitation of existing interpretability methods (like attention weights) by introducing **Transfer Entropy (TE)** to measure directional information flow and causal dependency within Transformers. Attention weights only reflect probability mass allocation, failing to capture true causal influence or information redundancy. The TE framework provides a **more principled and theoretically grounded** tool for understanding how information is processed and transferred across the Transformer hierarchy.

2.  **S2: Application of Information Flow Analysis to Practical Efficiency Improvement.**
    This work extends information flow analysis beyond purely explanatory research into practical model efficiency improvement. The authors design a **novel pruning strategy** based on identifying layers with low redundant information flow signaled by TE. The experiments demonstrate that this TE-based strategy achieves **comparable or superior performance** to existing pruning methods across various models (e.g., RoBERTa and T5) and tasks, successfully translating information-theoretic insights into an actionable model optimization technique.

weaknesses.value:
## Weaknesses

1.  **W1: Quantitative Reliability Compromised by Linear Approximation.**
    The core measure, Transfer Entropy (TE), is deemed **intractable** due to the high-dimensional, non-linear nature of Transformer hidden states. The authors resort to a \textbf{Jacobian Linear-Gaussian Approximation} or a \textbf{Cosine-Similarity Approximation}.
    * Given the highly non-linear nature of deep models, this strong linearity assumption fundamentally \textbf{violates the theoretical rigor} of the information-theoretic measure.
    * This approximation casts serious doubt on the reliability and quantitative accuracy of all subsequent findings derived from TE, such as the layer redundancy analysis and the proposed pruning strategy.

2.  **W2: Discrepancy in Interpreting Layerwise Information Flow (Training vs. Inference).**
    The layerwise TE, $TE_l(t)$, is defined to track information flow across **two consecutive training steps** $t$ and $t+1$. This captures dependencies in **training dynamics** (i.e., how back-propagated updates propagate).
    * This definition is conceptually distinct from the functional information flow during a single **inference** forward pass.
    * The paper fails to clearly justify why redundancy identified in the *propagation of training updates* robustly translates to a reliable signal for pruning layers during *inference*, potentially leading to a disconnect between the measured quantity and the claimed functional importance.

3.  **W3: Narrow Scope of VLM Experiments and Limited Generalizability.**
    The VLM analysis is only demonstrated on **CLIP ViT-B/16**, a relatively older and non-generative VLM architecture.
    * The conclusions regarding information flow in the vision and text encoders are thus of \textbf{severely limited generalizability}.
    * The framework's utility must be proven on more modern, mainstream **large generative VLMs** (like LLaVA or BLIP-2) which feature complex cross-attention mechanisms, which are the primary site of multimodal information exchange.

questions.value:
## Questions

1.  **Q1: Justification for Linear/Cosine Approximation on Non-linear Activation.**
    The cornerstone of this work is the use of Transfer Entropy (TE) via either a Jacobian Linear-Gaussian Approximation or a Cosine-Similarity Approximation. Transformers are inherently highly non-linear. The authors must rigorously justify why a \textbf{linear assumption} is sufficient and theoretically sound for high-dimensional, non-linear hidden states. Is there an empirical validation showing that the approximation error for TE (relative to a computationally infeasible exact calculation) remains within an acceptable bound, especially at deeper layers where non-linearity accumulates?

2.  **Q2: Disconnect between TE (Training Dynamics) and Pruning (Inference Functionality).**
    The paper defines layerwise TE ($TE_l(t)$) based on two consecutive training steps ($t$ and $t+1$), capturing dependencies in the \textbf{gradient propagation} (training dynamics). Pruning, however, requires identifying layers that are functionally redundant during a single \textbf{inference forward pass}.
    * Please provide a clear theoretical argument or empirical evidence to bridge this gap: Why does measuring the redundancy of *update signals* reliably map to the functional redundancy of *hidden layer activations*?
    * Have the authors explored defining TE between layer $l$ and $l+1$ *during a single forward pass* (i.e., conditional on the input $x$) to more directly measure functional information flow?

3.  **Q3: Generalizability and Applicability to Generative VLMs.**
    The VLM analysis is limited to CLIP ViT-B/16, which lacks the complex generative decoder and cross-attention mechanisms central to modern VLMs (e.g., LLaVA, BLIP-2).
    * Is the proposed TE framework computationally tractable for **large generative VLMs** (e.g., Llama/Mistral-based architectures with 7B+ parameters)? Runtime analysis suggests potential bottlenecks.
    * How does the framework handle the TE flow across the \textbf{cross-attention block} (Vision $\rightarrow$ Language)? Analyzing this specific junction is critical for understanding multimodal fusion, yet it is absent from the current VLM case study.

4.  **Q4: Causality and Redundancy vs. True Functionality.**
    The pruning strategy relies on identifying layers with low TE (low causal flow) or high redundancy. Low TE implies a layer's output is highly independent of the previous layer's update, or that its information is already largely accounted for.
    * Is it possible that a layer with \textbf{low TE} (i.e., low informational contribution from the previous layer's update) is actually performing a \textbf{critical non-linear transformation} on the existing information, making it essential for final output?
    * How is the risk of \textbf{pruning a functionally critical layer} based solely on low TE signals mitigated in the proposed strategy?

title.value: Response to Reviewer Comments on TE Approximation, Pruning, and VLM Generalizability

comment.value:
We are grateful for the reviewer’s insightful comments and address each point in the following response.

W1: Exact TE is infeasible for high-dimensional, nonlinear Transformer states, so our Jacobian Linear–Gaussian and cosine-similarity TE are intended as local approximations rather than exact information-theoretic quantities. The Jacobian approach is a standard first-order linearization around the operating point, while the cosine estimator provides a lightweight low-rank surrogate that preserves relative layerwise trends. Empirically, these proxies yield stable and consistent TE profiles across models and datasets, and we use them only for comparative analysis (e.g., layer ranking for pruning), not for estimating absolute TE. We clarify this scope and discuss approximation biases in the Appendix J.

W2: We acknowledge that our TE is computed across steps $t$ and $t{+}1$, capturing how upstream perturbations affect downstream activations during training. This reflects each layer’s local functional sensitivity. To verify that this training-time signal aligns with inference-time importance, we perform a reverse-TE pruning experiment in which we remove the four layers with the lowest TE. As shown in Row 6 of Table 1, pruning low-TE layers severely degrades performance, whereas pruning high-TE (redundant) layers preserves accuracy. This strong contrast indicates that TE remains a reliable indicator of functional importance for pruning, even though it is derived from training dynamics rather than a purely static inference view.

W3: We have expanded our VLM analysis beyond CLIP ViT-B/16 by adding a full information-flow study of LLaVA-7B (Appendix H.1), a modern generative VLM with deep cross-modal interactions. To further demonstrate generality across large models, we also include results for Llama-3B and Qwen-7B (Appendix G.6). These additions show that our TE framework extends to contemporary multimodal and decoder-based architectures.

Q1: Exact TE is intractable for high-dimensional, nonlinear transformers, so our goal is a local, comparative proxy rather than a fully faithful estimator. The Jacobian linear–Gaussian approximation (Sec. 4.2) linearizes the dynamics around the operating point, analogous to local Granger analysis, while the cosine estimator (Thm. 2) provides a lightweight rank-one surrogate using mini-batch finite differences. We clarify this modeling role in the revision and discuss limitations in Appendix J. As shown in Appendix F, these approximations preserve TE rankings in settings where exact TE is available. Since our use of TE is purely relative (e.g., layer ordering), pruning ablations further validate its functional relevance: TE-guided pruning preserves accuracy, whereas reverse-TE pruning significantly degrades it.

Q2: We clarify that although Sec. 4.2 introduces indices $t$ and $t{+}1$, in all experiments TE is computed from forward activations of a fixed network, not from SGD updates. The cosine estimator (Thm. 2) uses neighbouring samples/tokens within a mini-batch, so TE reflects local forward information flow $X_l \to X_{l+1}$ induced by small input perturbations. As noted in W2, our reverse-TE pruning experiment shows the link to inference functionality: removing low-TE layers severely hurts performance, while pruning high-TE layers preserves accuracy. This empirical asymmetry supports TE as a reliable pruning criterion.

Q3: We agree that evaluation on modern generative VLMs is important. In the revision, we extend our analysis to LLaVA-1.5-7B and report TE for the vision tower, language tower, and cross-modal vision$\rightarrow$text pathway (Appendix H.1), showing that the same three-part information-flow hierarchy holds in a 7B-parameter multimodal model. The cosine-based TE estimator remains tractable at this scale: it adds only two forward passes and batched dot products per mini-batch, yielding a small constant-time overhead, and we successfully run it on LLaVA-7B with a single A100 (Appendix H.1). Cross-modal fusion is handled explicitly by separating image and text tokens in each decoder layer and computing vision$\rightarrow$text TE at that interface.

Q4: Actually the pruning strategy relies on identifying layers with high-TE (pruning rules in page 6, Lines 290-297) and we explained the reasoning in page 5, Lines 267-269: when $TE_l(t)$ is large, the update at layer $l$ already explains most of the change at layer $l+1$. We agree that a layer with low TE could, in principle, perform a crucial non-linear transformation on already-present information. Notably, our reverse-TE experiment which prunes only low-TE layers causes severe accuracy degradation (Row 6 of Table 1), whereas high-TE pruning preserves performance (Row 2 of Table 1). This asymmetry supports TE as a practical redundancy signal, i.e., high $TE_l(t)$ means high redundancy between layer $l$ and $l+1$. We discuss the limitations of TE in Appendix J.

Thanks.  Abstractly, here is what I understand you are doing.  Let f and g be arbitrary functions.  You are considering the function h given by h(x) = f(x, g(x)) --- here g represents the transition mapping from time t to t+1, and f represents the transfer entropy: f(a,b) = I(b1; b2 | a2), where b = (b1, b2) and a = (a1, a2).  The local update that you are introducing around x_0 computes f(x_0, g(x_0 + delta x)), i.e., the perturbation is only applied to the input of g.  Is my understanding of your perturbation correct?

However, what you are interested in should be h(x_0 + delta x) = f(x_0 + delta x, g(x_0 + delta x)).  I do not see why you can simply "hold x fixed" (while changing the same x in the input to g) and hope to evaluate the correct quantity.  It may be the case that f(a,b) is only weakly influenced by a (much lesser than b), but if so, this needs to be shown (intuitively, I do not believe this is true).  Comments?

title.value: Thank You and Clarification on Local Perturbation of  y

comment.value:
Thank you for the detailed follow-up and for the illustrative counterexample.  We agree that if $\delta x_2$ is treated as a genuine random variable, then it cannot be removed from the conditioning in (35) in the way we previously suggested. 
Our earlier argument based on $y - J_{l+1}\delta x_2$ was therefore misleading, and we appreciate you pointing this out. 
To avoid confusion, we have removed this paragraph from Appendix A in the revised version.

Regarding your original question about $y = y_0 + \delta x_2$: in our setting $y = X_{l+1}^t$, and the quantity of interest is
$I\bigl(X_{l+1}^{t+1}; X_l^{t+1} \mid X_{l+1}^t\bigr)$. In the Jacobian linear–Gaussian approximation, we compute a local TE at a fixed past context $X_{l+1}^t = y_0$ and inject perturbations only into the innovation that drives the transition from time $t$ to $t{+}1$. That is, we approximate $I\bigl(X_{l+1}^{t+1}; X_l^{t+1} \mid X_{l+1}^t = y_0\bigr)$ with $y$ held fixed, and then average this local approximation over datapoints. Under this construction, we do not introduce a perturbation term $\delta x_2$ into $y$ at all; $y$ enters purely as the conditioning variable, consistent with the definition of conditional TE. 
We have clarified this modeling choice explicitly in Appendix A (and avoid notation that suggests we are perturbing $X_{l+1}^t$ itself) to prevent further confusion. We appreciate your feedback and would be very interested to hear if this revised explanation addresses your concern.

Thank you for this insightful question. We believe you are referring to why we take $y \approx y_0$ rather than $y \approx y_0 + J_{l+1}\delta x_2$. We now address this point in the revised Appendix A, in a new paragraph titled “Further clarification on perturbing $y$.” Please let us know if you have any further questions.

I thank the authors for re-writing Section 4, it is much more readable now.  I also appreciate the section on TE vs GC.

As for Theorem 1, thanks for adding details in the Appendix.  This confirms that you are looking at the effect of a perturbation at time t on the values at time t+1 --- my question then is, why is y approx y_0 and not y_0 + (delta x)_2, i.e., if Y is just X at layer l+1 at time t, which is perturbed, shouldn't you consider the new y and not the old y?  As it stands, you have Sigma uy = 0, but this is only because you take y to be deterministic, which is not true with the perturbation.  Am I missing something?

summary.value:
This paper introduces transfer entropy (TE) as a principled, information-theoretic measure to quantify directional information flow in Transformer-based models. The authors propose tractable estimators of TE for high-dimensional hidden states and apply them to both unimodal (RoBERTa, T5) and multimodal (CLIP ViT-B/16) architectures. The work positions TE as a complementary diagnostic to attention weights, providing insights into which components actually drive representational changes during training and fine-tuning.
At the layer level, the authors demonstrate that TE profiles reveal depth-dependent redundancy that can guide structured pruning with minimal performance degradation. They claim further analyses at the token and head levels, identifying “sink,” “broadcaster,” and “benign” roles and combining TE with CLS/EOT attention mass for role-aware head classification, but these are only presented in the appendix.
Overall, the paper aims to connect theoretical information flow measures with practical interpretability and compression of LLMs and VLMs.

strengths.value:
1. Novel formulation: Introducing transfer entropy as a directed information flow metric for Transformers is conceptually interesting and theoretically grounded. It adds a principled alternative to similarity- or attention-based interpretability measures.

2. Clear writing and presentation: Despite the mathematical content, the paper is readable and well structured. The main ideas are intuitive once introduced.

3. Strong empirical demonstration (for the layer-level part): The TE-based layer pruning experiments are thorough and convincing. The results show clear improvements over heuristic baselines in both interpretability and efficiency.

4. Broader vision: The discussion and conclusion sections thoughtfully position TE as a unifying tool for interpretability, model compression, and even safety-related analyses.

5. Methodological soundness: The proposed estimators are carefully derived, with complexity analysis and empirical validation (albeit mostly in the appendix).

weaknesses.value:
1. Incomplete coverage of claimed contributions:
The main text only discusses the layer-level experiments and pruning. The token-level and head-level analyses, explicitly listed as key contributions, are entirely relegated to the appendix and never referenced in the main paper. As a result, the main body does not substantiate all claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

2. Weak referencing to the appendix:
The main text does not guide the reader to where the omitted results can be found, making it non–self-contained. For a conference paper, the core contributions and evidence should be visible in the main submission, not buried without pointers.

3. Unexplained model choices:
The rationale for selecting specific models (RoBERTa, T5, CLIP) is only briefly justified by “unimodal vs. multimodal” variety, without deeper discussion on why these are representative or what their differences reveal.

4. Limited discussion of limitations or theoretical caveats:
While TE is powerful, its estimation under high-dimensional, correlated activations is nontrivial. A short discussion of possible biases or instability of the approximations would strengthen credibility.

5. Potentially overclaimed generality:
The conclusion presents TE as a “unified lens” for interpretability and compression, but given that large parts of the evidence are missing from the main text, this feels overstated.

questions.value:
1. Why were the token-level and head-level analyses (which are listed as major contributions) excluded from the main text? Could you briefly summarize their main findings or justify why they were omitted?
2. What are the main differences between the two TE approximations you propose in terms of bias, computational efficiency, and stability?
3. How generalizable are your pruning results beyond the chosen models and datasets (e.g., to decoder-only LLMs like GPT-style architectures)?
4. Could TE estimation feasibly be integrated into online training as suggested in future work, or is it still computationally too heavy?

summary.value: The paper proposes Transfer Entropy as a tool to understand and prune LLMs and VLMs. Contributions include justifying the use of Transfer Entropy, providing an approximation for Transfer Entropy and then empirical analysis of TE on models such as RoBERTa and CLIP. In doing so, they show that TE corroborates certain intuitions/hypotheses about the mechanisms in the transformer. Lastly, the paper also lays out one practical use of Transfer Entropy - to use as a heuristic for pruning.

strengths.value: The paper's usage of Transfer Entropy to analyze LLMs (and VLMs) is original to the best of my knowledge. Further their approximation of TE, laid out by Theorem 1 is also novel to the best of my knowledge. Their methodology and math is discussed clearly and in sufficient detail - it is largely sound. Experimental results are also promising: Not only are findings on RoBERTa are interesting - an inverted U shape, the application to pruning shows good results too.

weaknesses.value:
My main critique is that significance of the approach is not very strong, and is sometimes contradictory:
1. Claims around role-aware head classification are not backed by experimental results in the main body of the paper? I see a few plots in the Appendix, it would help to discuss them in more detail in Section 5. 
2. The experiments on RoBERTa are quite limited - using only GLUE benchmark. It is unclear to me if the same pattern holds on other benchmarks? I worry that it will not because of the results on CLIP model where the text encoder doesn't show an inverted U but the vision encoder shows something similar to what is seen on RoBERTa and GLUE. Further, in the appendix, it seems T5 doesn't follow the same trend either. I encourage the authors to focus on few claims and use the main body of the paper to substantiate their central claims.
3. I worry that pruning results on the CLIP and RoBERTa model aren't very valuable since the models are quite small already. We often struggle to prune larger models, such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, - finetuning these on an A100 is still possible for their smaller variants (< 7B parameters).
